newsitem.title: CHINA: China textile hopes rise after hard 1996.
newsitem.headline: China textile hopes rise after hard 1996.

text.p: Soaring cotton prices, falling tax rebates and strong international competition made 1996 a hard year for China's once-mighty textile exporters, but 1997 may be easier, the China Daily Business Weekly said on Sunday.
Textile exports slipped last year after years of powerful growth, the official newspaper said.
"We estimate annual exports in 1996 slid by three to five percent from the 1995 level," it quoted Yu Boge, vice president of the China National Textiles Import and Export Corp, as saying.

In the first 11 months of 1996, China exported $10.7 billion worth of half-finished textile products, down 13 percent from the year before, it said. Garment exports rose just 2.0 percent to $21.9 billion.
Domestic cotton prices that had soared past international levels to $1.05 a pound were a key factor behind the poor export performance, Yu said.

A cut in textile export tax rebates to nine percent from 14 percent had put extra pressure on exporters, already struggling to cope with intensified competition from countries such as Pakistan and India and regional trade protectionism, he said.
However, the prospects for exports in 1997 were more positive, Yu said.
"I think Chinese textiles exports will maintain an upward trend, which became clear in the latter part of last year," he said.
Textile exports had risen four to five percent year-on-year in the fourth quarter of 1996, compared with previous falls of up to 35.7 percent, he said.
Interest rate cuts last year and the allocation of 7.0 billion yuan ($843 million) by the Industrial and Commercial Bank of China to help firms buy cotton would help struggling exporters, he said.
Export tax rebates should be increased for textiles and their payment should be accelerated to further boost the sector, which employed more than 15 million workers, he said.
